Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here's what he thinks about the variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Images, and more new to iPhone 18 Pro.

Stalman takes a deep dive into the variable aperture camera on iPhone 18 Pro

This year's iPhone 18 Pro brings several new features, including a 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, but the biggest camera upgrade is clearly the variable aperture system.

Other updates this year include Cinematic mode, Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Images, and further refinements to the Camera app's pro controls.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shares his thoughts on all of the new hardware and software features of the iPhone 18 Pro camera. With the review embargo now lifted, reviews are rolling out, including our own from 9to5Mac.

Stalman notes that, while he loved last year's Cosmic Orange on the iPhone 17 Pro, the color tended to produce reflections when shooting through glass. So, he suggests pro photographers consider Deep Sea Blue or Black, since those colors are less likely to introduce unwanted color casts into photos and video.

He also states upfront that this review is comparing the iPhone 18 Pro camera to the iPhone 15 Pro, and the review video itself was shot almost entirely on an iPhone 17 Pro.

On the headline upgrade to the main camera — the new variable aperture — Stalman says the feature is "a big step in making iPhone a real camera."

He also points out that the larger f/1.48 aperture lets more light hit the sensor, helping to keep ISO down in low-light situations and reducing how often Night mode kicks in.

This portion of the review showcases great photos of the aperture blades opening and closing. Stalman notes that Apple's design is unique, with the aperture blades sitting in front of the main lens element rather than being buried deep inside the optical stack like a traditional camera design would have it.

Stalman also says that the 4x zoom on iPhone 18 Pro (also on last year's iPhone) is a notable improvement over the 5x zoom on iPhone 16 Pro, since the 5x zoom could sometimes feel a little too tight in terms of focal length.

When it comes to features that may have "gone too far," he briefly touches on the new AI editing tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Re-Frame, noting that while they are technically impressive and produce convincing results, they alter the image so much that the final product no longer preserves the feel of the original.

Moving on to the new texture options on iPhone 18 Pro — Smooth Skin, Glow, and Film — Stalman demonstrates each at strengths ranging from 0 to 100. His verdict: Smooth Skin does a good job of lightly reducing skin texture rather than just blurring skin tones, while Glow delivers a diffused highlight bloom similar to a professional Black Pro-Mist filter.

He's also impressed with the grain and halation in Film mode, though he wishes Apple would give users more options to control the intensity of the grain.

The review also covers Apple Reference Images, iPhone Cinematic mode (along with why Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic video), the new Apple Log 2, and is interspersed with photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 15 Pro.
